s: Passage: observed; decided; caught; been; penalise; cancellation — "It has been observed that drivers have become more careless … The traffic police committee has decided … the traffic offenders will be caught immediately … It has been decided to penalise the first instance … and the second with the cancellation of the driving licence."

Part B (Direct–Indirect speech) is explanatory: in indirect speech we remove the inverted commas, add 'that', change the person of pronouns, shift the tense back (am → was) and change adverbs of nearness (now → then, here → there, today → that day, tomorrow → the next day); questions use asked/inquired + if/whether with statement word order; commands use told/ordered/requested + to-infinitive.
1. Tahira said (that) she worked in an office.
2. Jamila told me (that) she was going to clean the room.
3. Jaffer said (that) they liked the song.
4. Iman and Marva remarked (that) they needed new shoes.
5. Kamran told us (that) he could speak Spanish.
7. The teacher said (that) Rauf had never been to Karachi.
8. Luqman said to Gul (that) the train hadn't arrived on time.
9. Eyma said (that) she was sitting on the chair.
10. Nauman told us (that) Waleed didn't eat meat.
11. Hamid remarked (that) Abrahim and Naummy would travel to Kaghan.

shortQuestions: The central idea is the evil of racial prejudice and pride: Armand rejects his wife and child because he believes they are of mixed race, only to discover that the 'black blood' came from his own mother. The story shows how racism destroys love and humanity, and how pride blinds people.

Armand fell in love with Désirée at first sight, 'as if struck by a pistol shot'; his passion was so strong that he did not care about her unknown origin. He was proud of his own old and noble family name and felt he could give her his name, so her lack of family did not matter to him then.

Armand Aubigny is a rich, proud and passionate planter of an old Louisiana family. He is hot-tempered, harsh and cruel to his slaves; his love for Désirée is passionate but shallow. When he thinks his child is of mixed race, he becomes cold and cruel and drives Désirée away. He is a slave to racial prejudice and pride, and in the end he is shown to be the one with African ancestry.

His behaviour changed when the baby grew older and began to show features of African descent. Armand believed this came from Désirée, whose parentage was unknown; his racial pride was hurt, so he became cold, avoided her and the child and treated the slaves even more harshly.

Because Désirée was a foundling with no known family, while Armand was proud of his 'pure' white lineage. So the blame for the baby's dark features was put on her unknown origin — Armand never thought that the cause could be in his own family.

It means that Armand remembered, with sudden shame, that Désirée had no family name or known parentage; he felt she had brought disgrace to his proud and ancient name, and he blamed her nameless origin for the child's colour.

Alternate ending: Before Désirée leaves, Armand finds his mother's letter. Ashamed of his cruelty, he rushes to the bayou, brings Désirée and the baby back, asks her forgiveness and frees his slaves. He learns that love and humanity are more important than colour and race. (Any logical ending is accepted.)
activities: Summary — Désirée's Baby: Beginning — Désirée, a foundling, is adopted by Monsieur and Madame Valmondé. When she grows up, the proud and wealthy Armand Aubigny falls in love with her and marries her, not caring about her unknown origin. Middle — They have a son and Armand is happy, but after some months the baby begins to show signs of African ancestry. Armand turns cold and cruel, and tells Désirée that the child is not white, which means she is not white. Heartbroken, Désirée takes the baby and disappears into the bayou. End — Later Armand burns all her belongings, and in a drawer he finds an old letter from his mother to his father, thanking God that Armand would never know that his mother belonged to the race 'cursed with the brand of slavery'. The truth is that Armand himself is of mixed race.

Discussion guide — forms of 'racism' in our society: discrimination on the basis of caste and biradari, tribe or ethnicity, language and province, rich and poor (class), skin colour in marriage proposals, urban and rural, sectarian differences. Each group gives examples and suggests remedies — the Islamic teaching of equality (Al-Hujurat 13), education, awareness and laws.
